name: Vintage Copperplate Engraving
description: A nineteenth-century copperplate engraving plate: fine cross-hatched linework and stipple on aged cream paper, restrained two-tone ink with a muted deep-green wash, clearing around one central subject.
style_bible: An antique intaglio plate reproduced on paper, in the manner of a nineteenth-century copperplate engraving as it appeared in a journal or a learned volume. Medium and surface: the whole picture is built from line — fine, even, closely spaced cut lines that swell and taper with the form, crossed into a lattice where a tone deepens, and resolved into stipple where a surface needs grain rather than direction. There is no brush rendering, no wash modelling and no photographic texture anywhere. Colour: restrained two-tone ink — a warm black-brown key printed over aged cream paper — plus a single muted deep-green wash laid flat and a little unevenly behind the light passages, the way a plate was hand-coloured. The palette never extends beyond those two inks and the paper. Tone: value comes from line density alone. A half tone is one hatching layer, a deep tone is a second crossing layer, and only the darkest recesses take a third; the brightest highlights are bare paper. Light is clear and calm rather than theatrical, bright enough to keep every form legible. Ornament: the fine decorative rules, cartouches and plate numbers of the period are deliberately absent — no caption block, no plate number, no ruled margin. One clear central subject carries the picture in a calm, authoritative arrangement with room around it. Aged paper: a light, even foxing tone and a faint plate-mark impression are welcome; a torn, burnt or heavily stained sheet is not. Keep the contract content-independent: no fixed subject, place, era, wording or copied composition.
